text.p: Inchcape Bhd's core motor distribution business has so far been relatively unaffected by import of cars by unauthorised dealers, or "parallel importers", chief executive Jeremy Hobbins said on Thursday.
"We have been relatively unaffected by parallel importers at this point in time," Hobbins told Reuters in an interview.
Inchcape is the agent and distributor for Toyota, which is the top selling make in Singapore, as well as for Suzuki cars.
It also sells these two brands in Brunei where it also distributes Rover, Volkswagen and Audi.
Hobbins said many of the Toyota models that parallel importers brought into Singapore were not the same as those Inchcape distributed and the total number of rival imports had been relatively small.
Parallel importers brought in about 100-200 cars a year and this was a "small percentage" of Inchcape's market share of about 7,000 units a year, he said.
Hobbins said parallel imports tended to put more pressure on profit margins for the group's motor business but currently it was "not a major factor in our margins".
On passenger car sales so far this year, Hobbins said he expected the size of the total market this year would be very much the same as last year, which saw sales of about 35,000 to 36,000 cars.
"There have been some incremental COEs (Certificates of Entitlement) which have been issued by the government. They are largely, though not exclusively, in the commerical sector," said Hobbins.
Under Singapore laws, car sales are controlled by the government though the issue of car quotas or COEs.
A new car buyer needs to secure a COE through a tender before he can register a new car.

Total car sales in the first quarter were down 12 percent against the same period in 1996. Inchcape's car sales were down by a slightly larger 14 percent in the same period mainly due to a supply problem in January, said Hobbins.
He said company's stock of cars was insufficient to meet demand in January, but sales had been climbing since this stock problem has been solved.
Hobbins said the weaker yen had also allowed more room for negotiation with Toyota and Suzuki about the pricing of their products.

Hobbins said the sale of Lexus, Toyota's upmarket answer to Mercedes Benz cars, had been affected by the economic slowdown in Singapore, but sales were still averaging at about 25 to 30 units a month.
He dismissed market talk that Inchcape had a huge stock of Lexus cars. He said the inventory levels for the Lexus were at an acceptable two to three months stock.
Motors and motor financing contributed about 70 percent of the group's 1996 pre tax profit of Singapore $79.2 million.
